network.overall_strategy: This is a connected network of ten distinct candidate pathways, not a claim that ten end-to-end prebiotic syntheses of free cysteine have been demonstrated. P1-P6 combine two experimentally supported acetylation approaches with three experimentally supported sulfur-installation sequences. They converge on protected cysteinyl compounds; their subsequent hydrolysis and deacetylation to surviving free cysteine remain explicitly unvalidated. P7-P9 represent historical photochemical or discharge target-channel hypotheses, with the limitations of the reported product assignments preserved. P10 represents the reported trace-cysteine result of Hennet, Holm and Engel (1992), the clearest direct free-target evidence in the supplied research. Mercaptoacetaldehyde Strecker chemistry, unactivated serine dehydration and the high-barrier glycine-thioformaldehyde proposal are excluded because their documented limitations offer no advantage here. Starting molecules are declared boundary supplies, not substances whose geochemical production is established by this network. In particular, acetylating-agent availability and ferricyanide supply remain unresolved. All reactions exclude molecular oxygen. Surface solution chemistry requires UV-shielded water or covered pores, whereas photochemical branches require exposed gas-water interfaces followed by protected collection. Numerical conditions identified as proposed are experimental screening specifications, not reconstructed literature protocols or demonstrated productive conditions. No quantitative transfer efficiency, oxidant removal, endpoint yield or cysteine survival is assumed. Neutral formulas represent reference species; actual protonation depends on pH. The schema's intermediate role also covers coproducts. Empirical reaction nodes are balanced projections of a target-forming channel, not complete descriptions of complex product mixtures. The oxidative acetylation node additionally identifies its unverified inorganic-sulfur bookkeeping assumption.

reactions.name: Glycolaldehyde Strecker synthesis of serine nitrile

conditions.temperature: 300-310 K proposed surface window; the cited work describes room-temperature chemistry
conditions.other: Proposed screening conditions: glycolaldehyde 20 mM, total cyanide 40 mM, total ammonia/ammonium 0.20 M, pH 8-9, sampling over 1-24 h. These concentrations and times are not a reconstructed published protocol. Use covered, anoxic water; quantify cyanide volatilization, polymerization and iron complexation.

reactions.mechanism: Ammonia forms a carbonyl-derived imine, followed by cyanide addition to give serine nitrile with net water loss. Nitrogen and cyanide protonation equilibria are implicit.
reactions.reasoning: Foden et al. (2020) support glycolaldehyde Strecker chemistry as a productive source of serine nitrile. Patel et al. (2015) provide broader cyanosulfidic precursor context, not a complete cysteine synthesis. The numerical screening conditions above are proposed because the supplied report does not specify the original Strecker concentrations and residence time. Unlike direct mercaptoacetaldehyde Strecker chemistry, this step postpones installation of the self-reactive aminothiol functionality.

reactions.name: N,O-Acetylation using supplied N-acetylimidazole

conditions.other: Proposed screening conditions: serine nitrile 20 mM, N-acetylimidazole 80 mM, pH 7-8.5, 1-6 h. At least two acetyl equivalents are required by the net reaction. Monitor competing acetylating-agent hydrolysis and distinguish N-acetylation from complete N,O-diacetylation. Shield from UV.

reactions.mechanism: Two nucleophilic acyl substitutions transfer acetyl groups to the amino and hydroxyl groups; two imidazole molecules are released per diacetylated product. N-Acetylimidazole is consumed, not a catalyst.
reactions.reasoning: The supplied account of Foden et al. (2020) identifies N-acetylimidazole as an alternative acetylating system. It does not establish its natural abundance or assign the oxidative protocol's 91% yield to this alternative. This route avoids residual oxidant during sulfur installation but requires an independently supplied activated acetyl donor. The stated concentrations and timing are proposed screening values, not reported yields or a validated environmental sequence.

reactions.name: Oxidative thioacetate N,O-acetylation with explicit redox bookkeeping
agents: Hexacyanidoferrate(III), a consumed stoichiometric oxidant rather than a catalyst

conditions.temperature: 300-303 K surface analogue of the reported room-temperature experiment
conditions.other: Reported organic-product benchmark: up to 91% N,O-acetylation in 1 h. Proposed screening start: serine nitrile 20 mM, thioacetic acid 40-80 mM, ferricyanide 40-80 mM, pH 7-8. Exact published concentrations are not supplied. Before downstream sulfide addition, require independently measured oxidant exhaustion; a proposed carryover specification is ferricyanide below 1 micromolar, not an achieved result. Ferricyanide regeneration and lossless separation are not assumed.

reactions.mechanism: Oxidative thioacetate activation enables two acyl transfers. No particular acyl-disulfide intermediate is asserted as experimentally identified here. One formal atom- and charge-balanced sulfur-pool closure is: 8 serine nitrile + 16 thioacetic acid + 16 ferricyanide -> 8 N,O-diacetylserine nitrile + 8 H2S + S8 + 16 ferrocyanide + 16 H+. The H2S/S8 partition is a bookkeeping assumption, not a measured coproduct distribution; polysulfides may intervene.
reactions.reasoning: Foden et al. (2020) strongly support the acetylated organic product and the approximately 1 h benchmark. The supplied research does not resolve the complete inorganic sulfur product inventory, so the explicit sulfur closure above is provisional and must not be interpreted as an established elementary mechanism. Muchowska and Moran (2020) discuss broader interpretive limitations of nitrile-centered prebiotic chemistry. Finite ferricyanide can act without molecular oxygen, but its environmental supply, competition with abundant reduced iron and removal before thiol chemistry remain unresolved.

reactions.name: Acetate elimination to N-acetyldehydroalanine nitrile

conditions.temperature: 300-303 K surface analogue; reported experiment at room temperature
conditions.other: Reported benchmark: pH 8, approximately 4 days, 85% N-acetyldehydroalanine nitrile. Proposed substrate range 1-20 mM; exact reported concentration is not supplied. Maintain covered, anoxic water. Buffer-mediated proton transfers are implicit; no mineral catalyst is assigned.

reactions.mechanism: The nitrile increases alpha-proton acidity, enabling beta-elimination of acetate from the O-acetylated substrate. N-Acetyl protection suppresses rearrangement and unwanted aminonitrile chemistry.
reactions.reasoning: Foden et al. (2020) reported 85% formation after four days at pH 8 and room temperature. This is a demonstrated activation solution, unlike spontaneous dehydration of unprotected serine. Applying the result at 300-303 K or to the proposed concentration range is a small but unmeasured extrapolation; competing hydrolysis and environmental dilution still require measurement.

reactions.name: Sulfide capture and nitrile-to-thioamide conversion

conditions.pressure: Approximately 1 atm with locally replenished reduced sulfur
conditions.other: Proposed screen: activated nitrile 1 mM, total dissolved sulfide 10-20 mM, pH 7-8, sampling from 1 to 24 h. At least two sulfide equivalents are consumed in the represented product channel. The supplied report gives near-quantitative protected-product formation but not the complete concentration/time protocol. Exclude residual ferricyanide and direct UV.

reactions.mechanism: Sulfide adds at the beta carbon of the activated alkene. A second H2S equivalent converts the nitrile functionality into a thioamide, giving an N-acetylated cysteine thioamide rather than free cysteine.
reactions.reasoning: Foden et al. (2020) reported near-quantitative formation of the protected cysteine thioamide from N-acetyldehydroalanine nitrile and H2S. No mineral catalyst is required. This evidence supports sulfur installation, not subsequent free-cysteine production. Sulfide loss to gas exchange or FeS precipitation and thiol consumption by residual oxidant must be measured in an integrated system.

reactions.name: Thioacetate conjugate addition to the activated nitrile

conditions.temperature: 300-303 K surface analogue of room-temperature chemistry
conditions.other: Reported benchmark: pH 7 and approximately 12 h for quantitative thioester formation. Proposed screening concentrations: activated nitrile 1 mM and thioacetic acid/thioacetate 5-10 mM. These concentrations are not supplied as the original protocol. Maintain anoxia and UV shielding.

reactions.mechanism: Thioacetate undergoes conjugate addition to the terminal carbon of N-acetyldehydroalanine nitrile, installing sulfur as an S-acetyl-protected side chain.
reactions.reasoning: Foden et al. (2020) reported quantitative thioester formation in about 12 h at pH 7. The product is N,S-diacetylcysteine nitrile, not cysteine. The protected sulfur functionality provides two chemically distinct downstream options: ammonolysis or sulfide-mediated thiolysis.

reactions.name: Selective S-deacetylation by ammonolysis

conditions.other: Proposed screen: S-acetyl substrate 1 mM, total ammonia/ammonium 0.10 M, pH 8-9, 12-48 h. The supplied report gives a 77% product yield but not these exact operating conditions. Monitor preservation of N-acetyl protection and competing nitrile chemistry.

reactions.mechanism: Ammonia attacks the thioester acetyl carbonyl, releasing the side-chain thiol and producing acetamide while retaining the N-acetyl group.
reactions.reasoning: Foden et al. (2020) reported 77% formation of N-acetylcysteine nitrile by ammonolysis. This is a protected-nitrile yield, not a free-cysteine yield. Retaining N-acetyl protection is chemically important because premature formation of unprotected cysteine nitrile would reintroduce the self-reaction problem documented in the same study.

reactions.name: Sulfide-mediated S-deacetylation and thioamide formation

conditions.pressure: Approximately 1 atm with sustained local sulfide supply
conditions.other: Proposed screen: protected substrate 1 mM, total sulfide 10-20 mM, pH 7-8, 1-24 h. Two H2S equivalents are consumed in the represented net transformation. The reported 95% protected-product yield is not assigned to these proposed concentrations or times.

reactions.mechanism: Sulfide cleaves the side-chain S-acetyl group, regenerating thioacetic acid, and another sulfide equivalent converts the nitrile into the thioamide.
reactions.reasoning: Foden et al. (2020) reported 95% cysteine-thioamide formation through thiolysis. This is an experimentally supported alternative to ammonolysis and converges with direct sulfide capture at the same protected thioamide. It does not independently validate downstream hydrolysis or free-cysteine preservation.

reactions.name: Prospective protected-nitrile hydration to N-acetylcysteinamide
agents: Aqueous acid, serving as a proton-transfer catalyst

conditions.temperature: 350-370 K proposed screening window; no productive window established
conditions.other: Proposed screen: protected nitrile 1-5 mM, acid concentration 0.1-1 M, nominal pH 0-1, 24-168 h with time-resolved analysis. Use covered, anoxic water without drying. The required acid inventory and selective hydrolysis rate are not established geochemically.

reactions.mechanism: Acid-assisted water addition to the nitrile, followed by proton transfers, can formally produce the primary carboxamide while retaining N-acetyl protection.
reactions.reasoning: SPECULATIVE ENDPOINT STEP. Foden et al. (2020) establish the protected nitrile substrate, not selective conversion under these conditions. Conventional nitrile hydrolysis provides chemical plausibility, but the essential inequality—nitrile hydration faster than N-deacetylation and destructive sulfur chemistry—has not been demonstrated. The proposed window is a falsifiable experimental screen, not a claimed solution to the free-cysteine problem.

reactions.name: Prospective thioamide hydrolysis to N-acetylcysteinamide
agents: Aqueous acid, serving as a proton-transfer catalyst

conditions.temperature: 350-370 K proposed screening window; no productive window established
conditions.other: Proposed screen: protected thioamide 1-5 mM, acid 0.1-1 M, nominal pH 0-1, 24-168 h. Maintain anoxia and quantify both dissolved and evolved sulfide. Measure carboxamide, thioacid, deacetylated products and insoluble losses rather than assuming a single hydrolysis channel.

reactions.mechanism: The represented hydrolytic channel replaces thiocarbonyl sulfur with oxygen and releases H2S, producing the carboxamide. Competing cleavage to thioacid-containing products is possible and is not represented as a demonstrated route.
reactions.reasoning: SPECULATIVE ENDPOINT STEP. Foden et al. (2020) support the starting thioamide but do not establish selective production of this carboxamide in the proposed pool conditions. The net reaction is balanced and chemically conceivable, yet branching between oxygen/sulfur hydrolysis products and loss of N-acetyl protection remains unresolved. A high upstream thioamide yield cannot be propagated through this node as a cysteine yield.

reactions.name: Prospective primary-amide hydrolysis to N-acetylcysteine
agents: Aqueous acid, serving as a proton-transfer catalyst

conditions.other: Proposed screen: carboxamide 1-5 mM, acid 0.1-1 M, nominal pH 0-1, 24-168 h. Released nitrogen will predominantly be ammonium at this pH; NH3 is the neutral reference species used for net bookkeeping. Quantify competing hydrolysis of the N-acetyl amide.

reactions.mechanism: Water attacks the primary carboxamide, ultimately releasing ammonia/ammonium and producing the carboxylic acid while ideally retaining N-acetyl protection.
reactions.reasoning: SPECULATIVE ENDPOINT STEP. The supplied research does not demonstrate this selective hydrolysis. Foden et al. (2020) establish protected cysteinyl chemistry upstream, not the required relative hydrolysis rates of the two amide functionalities. N-Acetylcysteine is included as a chemically meaningful prospective intermediate, not as an experimentally established product of the complete proposed environmental sequence.

reactions.name: Prospective N-deacetylation and recovery of free cysteine
agents: Aqueous acid, serving as a proton-transfer catalyst

conditions.temperature: 360-370 K proposed hydrolysis screen, followed by cooling to 300-310 K
conditions.other: Proposed screen: N-acetylcysteine 1-5 mM, acid 0.1-1 M, nominal pH 0-1, 72-336 h with repeated sampling. Avoid drying, direct UV and oxidant carryover. After sampling, cool promptly and assess recovery in anoxic water at pH 3-5. These are test conditions, not a demonstrated natural recovery protocol.

reactions.mechanism: Hydrolysis of the N-acetyl amide releases acetic acid and the free amino group of cysteine. The molecular formula represents cysteine independently of its solution protonation state.
reactions.reasoning: SPECULATIVE, NETWORK-CONTROLLING ENDPOINT. Foden et al. (2020) establish protected cysteinyl products, not selective deacetylation followed by accumulation of free cysteine under these conditions. No supported rate constants, isolated yield or product-survival measurement is available in the supplied research. Formation must outcompete decomposition, metal capture and downstream thiol chemistry; otherwise P1-P6 do not achieve the specified free target. Anoxia prevents reliance on oxygen chemistry but does not itself guarantee preservation.

reactions.name: H2S-sensitized hydrocarbon photochemistry: historical cysteine-channel projection

conditions.other: Gas irradiation coupled to aqueous collection. Proposed, not reconstructed, partial pressures: CH4 0.30 atm, C2H6 0.10 atm, NH3 0.10 atm and H2S 0.05 atm, with water vapor and an inert balance. Proposed irradiation screen: 254 nm, 10^14-10^15 photons cm^-2 s^-1, 24-72 h. Actual historical spectral fluxes and mixture proportions are not supplied. Collect condensate in a UV-shielded anoxic reservoir and directly distinguish cysteine from cystine.

reactions.mechanism: H2S photolysis generates energetic hydrogen atoms and sulfur radicals that initiate an unresolved organic reaction network. A balanced target-channel projection is CH4 + C2H6 + NH3 + H2S + 2 H2O -> cysteine + 6 H2. This is not an elementary reaction or a claim that H2 is the only coproduct of the complete mixture.
reactions.reasoning: Sagan and Khare (1971), Khare and Sagan (1971), and Hong et al. (1974) provide historical evidence for sulfur-containing amino-acid photochemistry. The approximately 5 x 10^-5 quantum yield reported for the Sagan-Khare system concerns total amino acids, not cysteine. Cystine detection cannot be counted as free-cysteine detection, and this node does not assume oxygen-mediated cystine formation or an unmodeled cystine reduction. Product specificity, modern analytical confirmation and net accumulation remain limitations. Locally reducing plumes are more defensible than a globally methane-ammonia-rich atmosphere.

reactions.name: Methanethiol-sensitized hot-hydrogen photochemistry: unverified cysteine branch

conditions.other: Proposed screening mixture, not an attributed historical recipe: CH4 0.30 atm, CH3SH 0.01-0.05 atm and NH3 0.10 atm, with water vapor and inert balance. Proposed UV screen: 254 nm, 10^14-10^15 photons cm^-2 s^-1, 24-72 h. Collect into covered anoxic water. Measure cysteine, cystine and other organosulfur products separately.

reactions.mechanism: Methanethiol photolysis can generate energetic H atoms and sulfur-containing radicals. The unresolved target-channel projection 2 CH4 + CH3SH + NH3 + 2 H2O -> cysteine + 6 H2 conserves atoms but does not identify the molecular mechanism or establish product selectivity.
reactions.reasoning: Hong et al. (1974) examined hot-hydrogen chemistry initiated by H2S or methanethiol and reported total amino-acid quantum yields of approximately 2-4 x 10^-5. The supplied account mentions cysteine in the historical discussion but does not assign a verified cysteine yield specifically to the methanethiol arm or to this proposed mixture. Consequently, this is a distinct, experimentally motivated but UNVERIFIED target branch, not a second established cysteine synthesis. It is retained as an alternative simple-sulfur-feedstock hypothesis without inventing radical intermediates or a cysteine-specific quantum yield.

reactions.name: Reducing sulfur-containing discharge chemistry: conditional cysteine-channel projection

conditions.temperature: 300-370 K bulk collection zone; discharge electrons are nonthermal, with a separate near-boiling water source in the historical apparatus
conditions.pressure: Historical initial non-water gas partial pressures total approximately 695 mm Hg
conditions.other: Miller apparatus conditions summarized by Parker et al. (2011): CH4 258 mm Hg, H2S 100 mm Hg, NH3 250 mm Hg and CO2 87 mm Hg; 300 mL water, continuously boiled and sparked for 3 days. CO2 is part of the experimental gas inventory but is not assigned carbon provenance in this target-channel projection. Discharge energy deposition, in-run pH and original cysteine recovery are not supplied. A modern test would sample immediately and collect under anoxia rather than infer products after storage.

reactions.mechanism: Electrical discharge creates an unresolved radical, cyanide and carbonyl network. A formal target-channel projection is 3 CH4 + NH3 + H2S + 2 H2O -> cysteine + 7 H2. The equation does not establish an exclusive product distribution or the actual carbon and nitrogen sources within the full apparatus.
reactions.reasoning: Parker et al. (2011) provide the quoted Miller-type conditions and evidence for diverse organosulfur products, but found no surviving cysteine in the archived samples. Cysteamine and related products are suggestive, not direct confirmation of prior cysteine. Historical cysteine/cystine reports attributed to Lu and coworkers in the supplied review are not matched here to a verified original protocol and cannot validate this exact Miller mixture. This node is therefore a conditional target hypothesis associated with demonstrated sulfur-organic discharge chemistry, not a reproduced free-cysteine result.

reactions.name: Mineral-buffered hydrothermal mixture with reported trace cysteine
agents: Pyrite-pyrrhotite-magnetite assemblage: experimental redox-buffering and reactive mineral phases, not demonstrated cysteine-specific catalysts
Small amount of Pt: experimental apparatus/redox component; no cysteine-specific catalytic mechanism established

conditions.pressure: Approximately 10 atm under a CO2/H2 gas phase
conditions.other: Reported initial inventory: KCN 0.19 M, NH4Cl 0.23 M, formaldehyde 0.18 M and approximately 0.05 M Na2S in the sulfide-containing experiment. NH4Cl and the CO2/H2 gas phase are essential experimental context even though they are not assigned net consumption in the formal target projection. The supplied report does not provide run duration, pH, gas ratio, mineral loading or full analytical workup. Proposed replication sampling at 12, 24 and 72 h and rapid anoxic cooling are screening choices, not attributed historical methods. Exact replication requires the original experimental protocol.

reactions.mechanism: Empirical outlet from an unresolved, concentrated hydrothermal reaction mixture. The reference-species equation 2 formaldehyde + HCN + H2S -> cysteine is atom-balanced but does not establish a three-feedstock mechanism, isotope provenance or exclusive products. Aminonitrile formation, homologation and sulfur incorporation remain unresolved within this node.
reactions.reasoning: Hennet, Holm and Engel (1992) reported cysteine only at trace/present levels under the specified mineral-buffered conditions, alongside much larger glycine yields. Trace formation is genuine target evidence and is not rejected merely for being low yield. However, the authors did not intend the approximately 0.1-0.2 M reagent inventories to represent ordinary natural hydrothermal fluids. The minerals cannot be described as proven cysteine catalysts. Missing duration, pH and analytical-workup information prevent an exact reproduction claim or a distinction between in-reactor free cysteine and any workup-dependent contribution. High-temperature destruction and sulfur sequestration require direct measurement; this result does not validate the selective hydrolysis steps in P1-P6.

pathways.name: N-Acetylimidazole activation followed by direct sulfide capture
pathways.description: Glycolaldehyde supplies serine nitrile; N-acetylimidazole enables elimination and direct sulfide capture to a protected cysteine thioamide. Sulfur installation is experimentally supported. Thioamide hydrolysis, primary-amide hydrolysis and final N-deacetylation are prospective, unvalidated connections to free cysteine.

pathways.name: N-Acetylimidazole activation, thioacetate capture and ammonolysis
pathways.description: Thioacetate addition and ammonolysis produce N-acetylcysteine nitrile. This is a leading prospective completion route because it retains N-protection while attempting nitrile hydrolysis. Its protected-product evidence does not establish the selectivity or survival required at the three hydrolysis/deprotection nodes.

pathways.name: N-Acetylimidazole activation, thioacetate capture and thiolysis
pathways.description: The S-acetylated intermediate undergoes sulfide-mediated conversion to the protected cysteine thioamide. This experimentally supported sulfur-processing alternative shares P1's unresolved endpoint hydrolyses and is not independent evidence for free-cysteine recovery.

pathways.name: Oxidative thioacetate activation followed by direct sulfide capture
pathways.description: Oxidative acetylation replaces the N-acetylimidazole boundary requirement, followed by elimination and direct sulfide capture. The organic acetylation product is supported experimentally, while inorganic sulfur closure and oxidant exhaustion require verification. Free-cysteine production remains conditional on the endpoint hydrolyses.

pathways.name: Oxidative activation, thioacetate capture and ammonolysis
pathways.description: Oxidative acetylation feeds the protected-nitrile branch through thioacetate addition and ammonolysis. This is topologically distinct from P2 through its acetylating chemistry, not through a separately demonstrated free-target endpoint. Residual oxidant and selective nitrile-before-N-acetyl hydrolysis are controlling tests.

pathways.name: Oxidative activation, thioacetate capture and thiolysis
pathways.description: Oxidative acetylation is combined with thioacetate capture and sulfide-mediated thioamide formation. The pathway shares experimentally supported protected-product transformations with other branches, plus their unresolved conversion to surviving free cysteine. Its additional branch structure does not increase endpoint confidence.

pathways.name: H2S-sensitized hydrocarbon UV route
pathways.description: Historical gas-water photochemistry provides evidence for cysteine/cystine-class products from simple gases. The single empirical node intentionally leaves the unresolved intermediate network unexpanded. Free-cysteine identification and preservation must be established separately from cystine detection and total amino-acid quantum yield.

pathways.name: Methanethiol-sensitized hot-hydrogen alternative
pathways.description: A distinct sulfur-feedstock hypothesis motivated by methanethiol hot-hydrogen experiments. The supplied evidence does not establish a cysteine-specific result for this exact arm or proposed mixture; this is an explicitly unverified candidate, not an additional demonstrated synthesis.

pathways.name: Reducing sulfur-containing electrical-discharge route
pathways.description: A conditional cysteine channel within a Miller-type sulfur-organic discharge network. Historical sulfur-amino-acid claims motivate the hypothesis, but archived Miller material contained no surviving cysteine. The network does not convert inferred degradation products into a claimed direct target observation.

pathways.name: Reported trace-cysteine hydrothermal outlet
pathways.description: The mineral-buffered experiment of Hennet, Holm and Engel provides reported trace target evidence from a concentrated cyanide-ammonium-formaldehyde-sulfide inventory. This branch has the strongest direct free-target evidence in the supplied research, but its elementary mechanism, complete protocol and geochemical scalability remain unresolved.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: The sequence through N-acetylcysteine thioamide is strongly supported by Foden et al. (2020). Keeping the nitrogen protected until after conversion of the terminal nitrile-derived functionality is strategically coherent. However, rxn_010-rxn_012 remain plausible hydrolytic extensions rather than a demonstrated route to recovered free cysteine. Their rates, selectivity and compatibility with cysteine survival are unspecified. All reactions conserve atoms and charge under the supplied check.
suggestions: Determine the products and rates of thioamide hydrolysis before assuming selective formation of N-acetylcysteinamide.
Specify pH, temperature, concentration and residence time for each hydrolysis, then quantify surviving free cysteine through the complete sequence.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Foden et al. (2020) support thioacetate addition and ammonolysis to the protected cysteine nitrile. The proposed continuation uses recognizable nitrile and amide hydrolysis chemistry and avoids deprotecting cysteine nitrile intentionally. Nevertheless, productive hydration and subsequent deacetylation have not been demonstrated under the submitted surface conditions. Evidence for protected cysteinyl products cannot be treated as evidence for the final free-target yield.
suggestions: Establish a hydration protocol that preserves N-acetyl protection until the nitrile has been consumed.
Track nitrile, amide, N-acetylcysteine and free cysteine separately during an integrated experiment, including losses and competing products.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: The thioacetate-addition and sulfide-mediated conversion sequence aligns well with the experimentally supported protected-product chemistry. The inferred requirement for two H2S equivalents in rxn_008 is conservation-consistent. This route reaches the same thioamide as P1 and therefore shares its unresolved hydrolysis and deacetylation bottleneck; an alternative sulfur-installation sequence does not independently validate free-cysteine production.
suggestions: Measure thioamide hydrolysis in the actual sulfide/thioacetate-containing product mixture rather than only with purified substrate.
Demonstrate recovery of free cysteine after the complete hydrolytic sequence under explicitly specified anoxic conditions.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Oxidative thioacetate acetylation has experimental support, and rxn_003 is atom- and charge-balanceable. Its particular H2S/S8 coproduct distribution is nevertheless an unverified bookkeeping assumption, not an established experimental stoichiometry. Residual ferricyanide and proton production introduce redox and pH compatibility requirements before sulfide capture. Oxygen exclusion alone does not resolve these issues. The final three hydrolyses remain unvalidated.
suggestions: Determine ferricyanide consumption and inorganic sulfur products experimentally rather than assigning a fixed H2S/S8 partition.
Verify oxidant depletion and pH control before sulfide addition, then test the complete hydrolysis and free-cysteine recovery sequence.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: The protected-product transformations align with Foden et al. (2020), and the nitrile-to-carboxylate-before-deprotection strategy is coherent. Integration is less secure than the individual supported transformations: rxn_003 leaves uncertain sulfur speciation and oxidant carryover, while rxn_009, rxn_011 and rxn_012 lack demonstrated productive conditions. These are chemical and operational uncertainties, not conservation failures.
suggestions: Test thioacetate capture and ammonolysis using the actual oxidative-acetylation product mixture after measured oxidant depletion.
Specify ammonia activity and pH for selective S-deacetylation, then establish hydrolysis conditions that avoid premature N-deacetylation.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: The activation, elimination and sulfur-installation chemistry provides a credible route to protected cysteine thioamide. Confidence in the complete pathway is limited by the unmeasured sulfur bookkeeping in rxn_003, compatibility of its product mixture with subsequent reduced-sulfur chemistry, and the same unresolved endpoint hydrolyses encountered in P1, P3 and P4. The supplied balance check identifies no conservation violation.
suggestions: Characterize redox state and sulfur speciation across oxidative acetylation, thioacetate addition and sulfide treatment.
Validate the thioamide-to-free-cysteine sequence in the resulting full mixture, with time-resolved product and recovery measurements.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Sagan and Khare's historical experiments support sulfur-containing amino-acid photochemistry from closely matching gases. However, cystine observations and overall amino-acid quantum yields do not establish a cysteine-specific yield or surviving free cysteine under this network's collection conditions. The balanced empirical projection is acceptable as a hypothesis, but does not resolve those analytical uncertainties. Anoxia alone does not prevent radical-mediated thiol oxidation.
suggestions: Specify irradiation spectrum, photon dose, gas partial pressures and gas-water contact conditions.
Use isotope labeling and validated chromatography/mass spectrometry to distinguish cysteine from cystine, with separate measurements before and after protected collection.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Hong et al. (1974) support methanethiol-associated hot-hydrogen amino-acid chemistry, but the supplied findings do not securely establish free cysteine from this particular methane/methanethiol mixture. The network appropriately labels this branch unverified. Its balanced stoichiometry establishes conservation only, not the required carbon-carbon assembly, target assignment or productive operating conditions.
suggestions: Identify the exact historical gas mixture and cysteine-specific analytical evidence underlying this proposed branch.
Experimentally screen the stated mixture using labeled carbon sources, authentic cysteine standards and measured post-irradiation recovery.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Historical discharge studies provide qualified support for cysteine/cystine formation. Parker et al. (2011), however, found no surviving cysteine in archived Miller samples, and degradation products are not definitive evidence of the target. A locally reducing volcanic setting is plausible, but discharge parameters and the complete gas mixture are unspecified. The conditional empirical-channel description is appropriately cautious, yet target achievement remains uncertain.
suggestions: Specify gas composition, pressure, discharge energy, water temperature and reaction duration, distinguishing which cited experiment is being modeled.
Measure freshly formed cysteine and cystine directly and follow their loss during circulation, cooling and storage.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Hennet, Holm and Engel (1992) provide the strongest direct free-target evidence among these pathways through their reported trace cysteine. Trace production counts positively; no minimum yield is required. However, the balanced three-feed projection does not establish a mechanism, atom provenance or independence from the other experimental mixture components. The original concentrated, mineral-buffered conditions must be specified, and mineral involvement should not be presented as demonstrated cysteine-specific catalysis.
suggestions: Annotate the reported 150 degrees C and approximately 10 atm protocol, reagent concentrations, ammonium supply, CO2/H2 phase, mineral assemblage and TiO2/Pt apparatus components, distinguishing their roles.
Replicate the trace result with blanks, isotope-labeled feedstocks and validated cysteine identification, measuring recovery after cooling as well as formation.
Test whether the reported outcome persists when concentrations and mineral conditions are varied toward the proposed environmental setting.

evaluation.network_feedback: The network is structurally valid: its 28 molecule nodes and 16 reaction nodes are sufficient and connected, and molecule IDs are used consistently. The deterministic check establishes atom and charge conservation for every reaction after coefficient assignment; none of the problematic-reaction flags denotes a conservation violation. The larger coefficients in rxn_003 do not themselves imply an implausible concerted mechanism, although its particular sulfur-product partition remains unverified. Literature alignment is strong: supported protected-cysteinyl chemistry is distinguished from prospective hydrolysis, historical product assignments and reported trace free cysteine. Nevertheless, rxn_009-rxn_012 are shared, unvalidated endpoint extensions, while rxn_013-rxn_016 are empirical projections with differing levels of target-specific support. P10 ranks highest because the supplied study reports the actual free target, not because hydrothermal chemistry is intrinsically preferred. Declared starting materials are accepted as boundary supplies; their absence from an upstream synthesis is not penalized. Environmental confidence remains conditional because per-reaction pH, temperature, concentrations, residence times and energy parameters are largely unspecified. Oxidant depletion, hydrolysis selectivity and exposed-to-shielded collection require validation. No serial transfer between the parallel surface and hydrothermal branches is intrinsically required. Add reaction-specific citations and operating conditions, and prioritize integrated free-cysteine formation and survival measurements. The network is not approved at the required 0.9 threshold. Its pathway count and shared intermediates do not independently validate the unresolved target-forming steps.
